Environmental.draft:
### Energy Performance  
Samsung Electronics reported total energy consumption at business sites of 38,772 GWh in 2024 (DX Division: 4,180 GWh; DS Division: 34,592 GWh) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Electricity accounted for 32,084 GWh (82.7%) of this total, while other energy sources—including steam, LNG, LPG, petrol, and diesel—contributed 6,688 GWh [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Renewable energy consumption reached 10,069 GWh in 2024, representing a renewable energy transition rate of 31.4% globally [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. By division, the DX Division achieved a 93.4% transition rate (2,884 GWh), whereas the DS Division reached 24.8% (7,184 GWh) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. The company confirmed 100% renewable electricity usage across manufacturing sites in Korea, Vietnam, China, Brazil, Mexico, and India since 2022 via Green Pricing, PPAs (solar/wind), and REC purchases [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_24]. Energy intensity stood at 13.5 MWh per KRW 100 million sales in 2024, down from 15.4 in 2023 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157].

### Water Management  
Total water intake was 188,540,000 tonnes in 2024, comprising 187,639,000 tonnes of municipal (surface) water and 902,000 tonnes of groundwater [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. Wastewater discharge amounted to 152,109,000 tonnes, while water reuse totaled 125,463,000 tonnes—including 74,784,000 tonnes of ultra-pure water supply and 23,025,000 tonnes of recovery [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158]. At Korean manufacturing sites (Giheung, Hwaseong, Pyeongtaek, Cheonan, Onyang), water reuse reached 101,106,000 tonnes in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_65]. All Korean sites achieved Alliance for Water Stewardship (AWS) Platinum certification in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Suppliers’ water consumption was reported as 88,467,000 tonnes in 2024, based on the top 90% of suppliers by transaction scale [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158].

### Emissions Management  
Market-based Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions totaled 14,546,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024 (Scope 1: 342,000 tonnes; Scope 2: 106,000 tonnes) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. The DS Division’s Scope 1 and 2 emissions were 15,011,000 tonnes CO₂e (region-based) in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_152]. NF₃ emissions—newly disclosed in the 2025 Report—amounted to 1,245,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_152][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. Total Scope 3 emissions were 105,612,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024, with “Use of sold products” constituting the largest category (82,714,000 tonnes CO₂e) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_154]. Air pollutant emissions included NOₓ (729 tonnes), SOₓ (35 tonnes), and PM (90 tonnes) in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158].

### Waste Management  
Total waste generated across divisions was 1,348,979 tonnes in 2024 (DX: 322,144 tonnes; DS: 1,026,835 tonnes), comprising general waste (910,510 tonnes), hazardous waste (13,281 tonnes of ferrous metals; 35,909 tonnes of synthetic resin), and other categories [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. The company recovered 6.91 million tonnes of e-waste cumulatively from 2009 through end-2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_29][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_30]. In Korea, 99.0% recycling rate was achieved at manufacturing sites in 2024, with a target of 99.9% by 2025 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_41]. Twenty-two global sites pursued Platinum Zero Waste-to-Landfill validation, with Korea’s Gumi site and several international locations (e.g., Hungary, Vietnam) already certified Platinum [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_31].

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
Samsung Electronics integrates climate risk into its enterprise-wide risk management system, applying a four-step process: recognition → assessment → treatment → progress management [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_29][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Physical risks (e.g., drought, flood) and transition risks (e.g., carbon pricing, regulatory shifts) are assessed using IPCC, IEA, and NGFS scenarios [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_46]. Key metrics include Scope 1+2 emissions (target: net zero by 2030 for DX Division; 2050 for DS Division), renewable energy transition rate (target: 100% for all manufacturing sites by 2025), and water reuse (target: 109 million tonnes at Korean sites by 2030) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42].

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 302 Energy: Location-based Scope 2 emissions breakdown by country; energy from on-site renewables generation (e.g., solar PV capacity).  
GRI 303 Water: Water stress assessments per facility; water withdrawal intensity (e.g., m³/tonne of product).  
GRI 305 Emissions: Biogenic CO₂ emissions; methane and nitrous oxide emissions disaggregated by source (e.g., wastewater, refrigerants).  
GRI 306 Waste: Hazardous waste generation by type (e.g., solvent, heavy metal sludge); landfill diversion rates by site; e-waste collection volumes by country.

### Occupational Health and Safety  
Samsung Electronics reported a Lost-Time Injury Rate (LTIR) of 0.022% in 2024, down from 0.023% in 2023 and 0.033% in 2022, based on workplace accidents resulting in one or more days of absence (excluding daily life incidents) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. The supplier LTIR stood at 0.035% in 2024, a reduction from 0.064% in 2023 and 0.046% in 2022, measured for accidents occurring at Korean suppliers stationed at Samsung’s sites [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. No major incidents were recorded in 2022–2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. The company’s occupational health and safety management system covers all employees globally and extends to suppliers through audits, training, and the Supplier Environmental Safety Portal [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_76][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114]. In 2024, approximately 3,000 risk assessment experts were trained to strengthen hazard identification and mitigation capabilities [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_98].

### Training  
In 2024, Samsung Electronics delivered an average of 66.8 training hours per employee globally, up from 58.2 hours in 2023 and 52.1 hours in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. In Korea, the average was 61.2 hours per employee, compared to 77.5 hours in 2023 and 70.5 hours in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. Women received slightly more training than men: 69.0 hours versus 61.6 hours in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. Total training expenses amounted to KRW 240.4 billion in 2024 (KRW 100 million × 2,404), representing 0.08% of sales and 0.6% of personnel expenses [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. The company also operated 936 training sessions globally in 2024, including 522 in Korea and 414 outside Korea [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. Human rights training reached 95.7% of all employees in 2024, with offline completion at 98.8% and online at 93.4% [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_77].

### Diversity  
The global percentage of female employees rose to 33.6% in 2024, from 34.0% in 2023 and 35.2% in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. In Korea, women comprised 25.8% of the workforce in 2024, up from 25.3% in 2023 and 25.2% in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. At the executive level, women accounted for 7.4% of executives in 2024, consistent with 7.3% in 2023 and 6.9% in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. Employees with disabilities numbered 1,999 in Korea in 2024 (1.9% of the Korean workforce), up from 1,931 (1.8%) in 2023 and 1,732 (1.6%) in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. Samsung joined the Valuable 500 initiative in December 2024 to advance inclusion for people with disabilities [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_92].

### Supplier Social Assessment  
In 2024, 92% of Samsung’s global suppliers underwent comprehensive evaluation, with 75% rated “outstanding” — up from 71% in 2023 and 62% in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_148]. Among first-tier suppliers, 93% complied with working hour standards in 2024, recovering from 85% in 2023 and aligning with 2022’s 93% [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114]. Third-party audit compliance rates for non-discrimination stood at 100% for first-tier suppliers in 2024, down from 100% in 2023 but significantly higher than 92% for second-tier suppliers [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_150]. Forced labor special audits covered 53 suppliers across five countries in 2024, and USD 14,838 in recruitment fees was returned to 41 migrant workers [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114].

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 405-2 (ratio of basic salary and remuneration of women to men) is not quantitatively disclosed beyond regional gender pay gap references (e.g., UK, France, Brazil) without consolidated global ratios [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_95]. TCFD Strategy disclosures on social impacts of climate transition — including workforce reskilling for low-carbon transitions, community engagement in decarbonisation, or just transition planning — are absent from the provided context. GRI 403-7 (prevention/mitigation of OHS impacts via business relationships) lacks specific metrics on supplier-level interventions beyond LTIR and audit rates. GRI 414-2 (actions taken in response to non-compliance in supplier assessments) is not detailed with corrective action timelines or outcomes.

Governance.draft:
### Board Composition and Oversight Structure  
As of the end of March 2025, Samsung Electronics’ Board of Directors comprises 3 internal directors and 6 independent directors, with the roles of Board Chair and CEO formally separated to strengthen independence and transparency; independent director Je-Yoon Shin serves as Chair [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. All 6 independent directors participate in the Sustainability Committee — a dedicated committee under the Board established in July 2021 to oversee environmental, social, and governance (ESG) strategy, risk management, and shareholder value creation [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. The Board serves as the highest decision-making body for sustainable management activities, including climate-related risks and opportunities, and approves long-term environmental strategies such as the “New Environmental Strategy” resolved in September 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_177][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_11].  

### Anti-Corruption Governance and Compliance Systems  
Samsung Electronics maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward corruption and bribery, grounded in its Global Anti-Corruption and Bribery Policy [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. The corporate Compliance Team, led by the Chief Compliance Officer, attends all Board and Management Committee meetings to support transparent decision-making and reports major issues directly to the Board [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. The Samsung Compliance Committee — an independent external body launched in February 2020 — advises seven major Samsung Group member companies, including Samsung Electronics, on strengthening compliance monitoring and control functions [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. In 2024, the company conducted compliance audits across multiple operational domains, including global manufacturing sites (Q3) and external technology sourcing channels (Q4), with anti-corruption explicitly cited as a key audit focus area [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137]. A total of 1,238 compliance-related whistleblowing cases were reported in 2024, alongside 930 ethics-related cases [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137]. All employees — including contract and part-time workers — receive annual compliance training covering anti-corruption and fair trade; in 2024, 138,414 individuals completed such training [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137].  

### Integration of Climate Risk into Enterprise Risk Management  
Climate-related risks and opportunities are systematically integrated into Samsung Electronics’ enterprise risk management system [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181]. The company employs a structured Climate-Related Risk and Opportunity Analysis Process that includes forming a risk/opportunity pool, conducting scenario analysis (using IPCC, IEA, and NGFS scenarios), assessing financial impacts, and evaluating mitigation and adaptation capacity [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_44][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18]. Physical risks (e.g., floods, typhoons, droughts, wildfires, extreme heat) impact operations across short-, medium-, and long-term horizons, while transition risks (e.g., rising carbon credit costs, energy price volatility) and opportunities (e.g., demand for low-carbon products, renewable energy adoption) predominantly affect the medium- to long-term [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_178][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_43]. Key findings from this analysis are reported to the Sustainability Committee and ESG Management Council for deliberation and response planning [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181]. Additionally, acute climate events trigger emergency response protocols aligned with ISO 22301 Business Continuity Management System standards to minimize disruption and restore operations promptly [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_44].  

### Performance Evaluation and Accountability Mechanisms  
Sustainability indicators — including greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction, renewable energy transition, and power savings — have been embedded in performance evaluation systems for both organizations and executives since 2021 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. For example, climate-related KPIs are reflected in the management team’s performance metrics, and the DX Division’s Sustainability Council met three times in 2024 to review annual plans and progress across business units [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_14]. The DS Division’s Carbon Reduction Committee oversees GHG emission monitoring and climate change response execution, while the Environmental Safety Meetings supervise GHG emissions management [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_14][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_40]. In 2024, Samsung Electronics reported Scope 1 and 2 emissions of 14.55 million tonnes CO₂e (market-based) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_40], with emissions data verified per GRI and GHG Protocol standards [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_171].  

### Not covered in source material  
The source material does not disclose: (1) formal evaluation of the Board’s own performance (GRI 2-18); (2) remuneration policies or processes for directors (GRI 2-19–2-21); (3) collective knowledge profile of the Board (GRI 2-17); (4) verification of Scope 3 emissions methodology beyond disclosure of verification statements (GRI 205-1 requires scope of assessment); (5) quantitative data on confirmed corruption incidents and remedial actions taken (GRI 205-3); (6) tax governance structure or country-by-country reporting beyond a reference to page 62 (GRI 207-2–207-4).

### Energy Performance  
Samsung Electronics reported total energy consumption at business sites of 38,772 GWh in 2024 (DX Division: 4,180 GWh; DS Division: 34,592 GWh) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Electricity accounted for 32,084 GWh (82.7%) of this total, while other energy sources—including steam, LNG, LPG, petrol, and diesel—contributed 6,688 GWh [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Renewable energy consumption reached 10,069 GWh in 2024, representing a renewable energy transition rate of 31.4% of total energy consumption [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. By division, the DX Division consumed 2,884 GWh of renewable energy out of 3,088 GWh of electricity (93.4% of *electricity*, not total energy) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]; the DS Division consumed 7,184 GWh of renewable energy out of 28,996 GWh of electricity (24.8% of *electricity*) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. The company confirmed 100% renewable electricity usage across manufacturing sites in Korea, Vietnam, China, Brazil, Mexico, and India since 2022 via Green Pricing, PPAs (solar/wind), and REC purchases [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_24]. Energy intensity stood at 13.5 MWh per KRW 100 million sales in 2024, calculated as energy consumption at business sites (MWh) divided by consolidated sales of DX and DS Divisions (KRW 100 million) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. Location-based Scope 2 emissions are not disclosed in the source material.

### Water Management  
Total water intake was 188,540,000 tonnes in 2024, comprising 187,639,000 tonnes of municipal (surface) water and 902,000 tonnes of groundwater [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. Wastewater discharge amounted to 152,109,000 tonnes, while water reuse totaled 125,463,000 tonnes—including 74,784,000 tonnes of ultra-pure water supply and 23,025,000 tonnes of recovery [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158]. At Korean manufacturing sites (Giheung, Hwaseong, Pyeongtaek, Cheonan, Onyang), water reuse reached 101,106,000 tonnes in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_65]. This reuse includes internal recirculation of ultra-pure water within semiconductor manufacturing processes and is not drawn from external freshwater sources [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_65]. All Korean sites achieved Alliance for Water Stewardship (AWS) Platinum certification in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Suppliers’ water consumption was reported as 88,467,000 tonnes in 2024, based on the top 90% of suppliers by transaction scale [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158]. Water withdrawal intensity (e.g., m³ per unit of output) and facility-level water stress assessments are not disclosed in the source material.

### Emissions Management  
Market-based Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions totaled 14,546,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024 (Scope 1: 342,000 tonnes; Scope 2: 106,000 tonnes) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. The DS Division’s “region-based” Scope 1 and 2 emissions were reported separately as 15,011,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024 — a distinct calculation basis using country-specific emission factors rather than market-based instruments (e.g., RECs, PPAs); therefore, the figures are not directly comparable and reflect different accounting methodologies [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_152]. NF₃ emissions—newly disclosed in the 2025 Report—amounted to 1,245,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024 and are included in the total market-based Scope 1 emissions figure [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_152][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. Total Scope 3 emissions were 105,612,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024, with “Use of sold products” constituting 82,714,000 tonnes CO₂e — a decrease of 402,000 tonnes CO₂e from 83,116,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2023, attributed to product energy efficiency improvements [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_154][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_164]. Air pollutant emissions included NOₓ (729 tonnes), SOₓ (35 tonnes), and PM (90 tonnes) in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158]. Biogenic CO₂ emissions and disaggregated methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions by source (e.g., wastewater, refrigerants, leakage) are not disclosed in the source material.

### Waste Management  
Total waste generated across divisions was 1,348,979 tonnes in 2024 (DX: 322,144 tonnes; DS: 1,026,835 tonnes), comprising general waste (910,510 tonnes), hazardous waste (13,281 tonnes of ferrous metals; 35,909 tonnes of synthetic resin), and other categories [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. In 2024, Samsung collected 690,900 tonnes of e-waste, contributing to a cumulative total of 6,910,000 tonnes recovered from 2009 through end-2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_30]. The company achieved a 99.0% recycling rate at Korean manufacturing sites in 2024, with a target of 99.9% by 2025 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_41]. Twenty-two global sites pursued Platinum Zero Waste-to-Landfill validation, with Korea’s Gumi site and several international locations (e.g., Hungary, Vietnam) already certified Platinum [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_31]. Hazardous waste generation by type (e.g., solvent, heavy metal sludge), landfill diversion rates by site, and e-waste collection volumes by country are not disclosed in the source material.

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
Samsung Electronics integrates climate risk into its enterprise-wide risk management system, applying a four-step process: recognition → assessment → treatment → progress management [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_29][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Physical risks (e.g., drought, flood) and transition risks (e.g., carbon pricing, regulatory shifts) are assessed using IPCC, IEA, and NGFS scenarios [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_46]. Key metrics include Scope 1+2 emissions (target: net zero by 2030 for DX Division; 2050 for DS Division), renewable energy transition rate (target: 100% for all manufacturing sites by 2025), and water reuse (target: 109 million tonnes at Korean sites by 2030) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Financial impact quantification from climate scenarios (e.g., cost implications of drought or carbon pricing) is disclosed qualitatively but not with numerical estimates [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_46][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_20].

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 302 Energy: Location-based Scope 2 emissions breakdown by country; energy from on-site renewables generation (e.g., solar PV capacity); definition of sales metric used for energy intensity beyond “sales of DX division (absolute value) + sales of DS division (absolute value)” [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157].  
GRI 303 Water: Water stress assessments per facility; water withdrawal intensity (e.g., m³/tonne of product or wafer); clarification of whether ultra-pure water supply volume (74.8M tonnes) represents internal recirculation only or includes external intake.  
GRI 305 Emissions: Biogenic CO₂ emissions; methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions disaggregated by source (e.g., wastewater treatment, refrigerants, leakage); methodological uncertainties in NF₃ measurement; confirmation that NF₃ is fully embedded in Scope 1 totals.  
GRI 306 Waste: Hazardous waste generation by type (e.g., solvent, heavy metal sludge); landfill diversion rates by site; e-waste collection volumes by country; annual e-waste collection volumes prior to 2024 beyond the summary chart [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_30].

### Occupational Health and Safety  
Samsung Electronics reported a Lost-Time Injury Rate (LTIR) of 0.022% in 2024, down from 0.023% in 2023 and 0.033% in 2022, based on workplace accidents resulting in one or more days of absence (excluding daily life incidents) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. The supplier LTIR stood at 0.035% in 2024, a reduction from 0.064% in 2023 and 0.046% in 2022, measured for accidents occurring at Korean suppliers stationed at Samsung’s sites [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. No major incidents were recorded in 2022–2024; however, the report does not define “major incident” using an external standard (e.g., OSHA, ILO) or specify a severity threshold (e.g., fatalities, hospitalizations, regulatory citations), nor does it disclose whether this reflects zero occurrences or non-reporting due to threshold exclusions [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. The company’s occupational health and safety management system covers all employees globally and extends to suppliers through audits, training, and the Supplier Environmental Safety Portal [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_76][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114]. In 2024, approximately 3,000 risk assessment experts were trained to strengthen hazard identification and mitigation capabilities [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_98]. Samsung has set a goal to strengthen on-site partner companies’ safety and health capabilities and management systems by 2030 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114].

### Training  
In 2024, Samsung Electronics delivered an average of 66.8 training hours per employee globally, up from 58.2 hours in 2023 and 52.1 hours in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. In Korea, the average was 61.2 hours per employee, down from 77.5 hours in 2023 and 70.5 hours in 2022 — a 16.3-hour reduction year-on-year — though the context provides no explanation for this decline [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. Women received slightly more training than men: 69.0 hours versus 61.6 hours in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. Total training expenses amounted to KRW 240.4 billion in 2024 (KRW 100 million × 2,404), representing 0.08% of sales and 0.6% of personnel expenses [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. The company operated 936 training sessions globally in 2024, including 522 in Korea and 414 outside Korea [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. Human rights training reached 95.7% of all employees in 2024, with offline completion at 98.8% and online at 93.4% [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_77]. No time-bound, quantified target for average training hours (e.g., “achieve 75 hours per employee by 2027”) is disclosed in the source material.

### Diversity  
The global percentage of female employees declined to 33.6% in 2024, from 34.0% in 2023 and 35.2% in 2022 — a cumulative decrease of 1.6 percentage points over three years — yet the context offers no analysis of drivers behind this trend (e.g., hiring patterns, attrition differentials, regional composition shifts) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. In Korea, women comprised 25.8% of the workforce in 2024, up from 25.3% in 2023 and 25.2% in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. At the executive level, women accounted for 7.4% of executives in 2024, consistent with 7.3% in 2023 and 6.9% in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. Employees with disabilities numbered 1,999 in Korea in 2024 (1.9% of the Korean workforce), up from 1,931 (1.8%) in 2023 and 1,732 (1.6%) in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. Samsung joined the Valuable 500 initiative in December 2024 to advance inclusion for people with disabilities [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_92]. The ratio of basic salary and remuneration of women to men (GRI 405-2) is not disclosed globally; only regional gender pay gap figures are referenced for the UK, France, and Brazil, with no consolidated global ratio provided [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_95].

### Supplier Social Assessment  
In 2024, 92% of Samsung’s global suppliers underwent comprehensive evaluation, with 75% rated “outstanding” — up from 71% in 2023 and 62% in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_148]. However, the context does not define the criteria or methodology used to determine “comprehensive evaluation” (e.g., whether it includes RBA-aligned self-assessments, third-party audits, certification verification, or risk-tier weighting), nor does it clarify whether the 92% refers to supplier count, spend-weighted coverage, or risk-based sampling [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_148][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_110]. Among first-tier suppliers, 93% complied with working hour standards in 2024, recovering from 85% in 2023 and aligning with 2022’s 93%; the context attributes the 2023 dip to “temporary increase in factory operating rates after the end of the COVID-19 pandemic”, and notes that operations stabilized by 2024, restoring compliance [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114]. Third-party audit compliance rates for non-discrimination stood at 100% for first-tier suppliers in 2024, down from 100% in 2023 but significantly higher than 92% for second-tier suppliers [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_150]. Forced labor special audits covered 53 suppliers across five countries in 2024, and USD 14,838 in recruitment fees was returned to 41 migrant workers [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114]. No corrective actions taken in response to supplier social non-compliance (e.g., capacity-building mandates, contract revisions, termination) are described beyond fee reimbursements and training [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_150].

### TCFD Strategy (Social Impacts of Climate Transition)  
The context confirms Samsung Electronics conducted climate scenario analysis using IPCC, IEA, and NGFS frameworks to assess physical and transition risks and opportunities, including financial impacts on operations, supply chain, and product demand [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_179][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_20]. It identifies transition opportunities such as “increases in demand for low-carbon products and services” and “use of renewable energy” [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_179], and notes investments in water reuse to mitigate drought-related cost risks [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_179]. However, no disclosure addresses the *social* dimensions of climate transition — including workforce reskilling for green jobs, community engagement in decarbonisation, just transition planning for affected workers or regions, or social safeguards in low-carbon investment decisions — is present in the provided material [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_179].

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 405-2 (ratio of basic salary and remuneration of women to men) is not disclosed globally; only regional gender pay gap data for the UK, France, and Brazil is referenced without a consolidated global figure [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_95]. GRI 403-7 (prevention and mitigation of occupational health and safety impacts directly linked by business relationships) lacks specific metrics on supplier-level interventions beyond LTIR and audit rates; no data on joint safety programs, contractual OHS clauses, or remediation timelines for supplier incidents is provided [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_76][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114]. GRI 414-2 (negative social impacts in the supply chain and actions taken) is not detailed with corrective action timelines, root-cause analyses, or outcomes beyond forced labor fee reimbursements and working hour compliance recovery [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_150]. TCFD Strategy disclosures on social impacts of climate transition — including workforce reskilling, community engagement, or just transition planning — are absent from the provided context [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_179]. No time-bound, quantified targets (e.g., “reduce LTIR to 0.015% by 2027”, “achieve 40% female executives by 2030”) are disclosed for any Social performance indicator.

### Board Composition and Oversight Structure  
As of the end of March 2025, Samsung Electronics’ Board of Directors comprises 3 internal directors and 6 independent directors, with the roles of Board Chair and CEO formally separated to strengthen independence and transparency; independent director Je-Yoon Shin serves as Chair [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. The Board’s collective expertise includes extensive knowledge or experience in finance, law, IT (robotics, AI, semiconductors), risk management, public sector, and sustainable management — reflecting deliberate consideration of functional diversity, gender, and nationality in director appointments [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. Two of the six independent directors are women, supporting balanced decision-making [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. All independent directors serve on the Sustainability Committee — a dedicated committee under the Board established in July 2021 to oversee environmental, social, and governance (ESG) strategy, risk management, and shareholder value creation [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. The Board approves long-term environmental strategies such as the “New Environmental Strategy”, resolved in September 2022, which encompasses climate change response and resource circularity goals [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_177][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_11]. Since 2023, key achievements related to these goals have been reviewed annually by the Sustainability Committee as part of its formal agenda [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_11][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_40].

### Anti-Corruption Governance and Compliance Systems  
Samsung Electronics maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward corruption and bribery, grounded in its Global Anti-Corruption and Bribery Policy [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. The corporate Compliance Team, led by the Chief Compliance Officer, attends all Board and Management Committee meetings to support transparent decision-making and reports major issues directly to the Board [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. The Samsung Compliance Committee — an independent external body launched in February 2020 — advises seven major Samsung Group member companies, including Samsung Electronics, on strengthening compliance monitoring and control functions [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. In 2024, anti-corruption was explicitly cited as a focus area in compliance audits of global manufacturing sites (Q3) and external technology sourcing channels (Q4) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137]. A total of 1,238 compliance-related whistleblowing cases and 930 ethics-related cases were reported in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137]. All employees — including contract and part-time workers — receive annual compliance training covering anti-corruption and fair trade; in 2024, 138,414 individuals completed such training [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137]. The scope of operations assessed for corruption risks is not specified in the source material [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_173]. Confirmed incidents of corruption and actions taken are not disclosed [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_173].

### Integration of Climate Risk into Enterprise Risk Management  
Climate-related risks and opportunities are systematically integrated into Samsung Electronics’ enterprise risk management system [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181]. The company employs a structured Climate-Related Risk and Opportunity Analysis Process that includes forming a risk/opportunity pool, conducting scenario analysis (using IPCC, IEA, and NGFS scenarios), assessing financial impacts, and evaluating mitigation and adaptation capacity [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_44][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18]. Physical risks (e.g., floods, typhoons, droughts, wildfires, extreme heat) impact operations across short-, medium-, and long-term horizons, while transition risks (e.g., rising carbon credit costs, energy price volatility) and opportunities (e.g., demand for low-carbon products, renewable energy adoption) predominantly affect the medium- to long-term [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_178][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_43]. Key findings from this analysis are reported to the Sustainability Committee and ESG Management Council for deliberation and response planning [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181]. Acute climate events trigger emergency response protocols aligned with ISO 22301 Business Continuity Management System standards to minimize disruption and restore operations promptly [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_44]. Quantified financial targets for climate risk mitigation or opportunity capture are not disclosed [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_178].

### Performance Evaluation and Accountability Mechanisms  
Sustainability indicators — including greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction, renewable energy transition, and power savings — have been embedded in performance evaluation systems for both organizations and executives since 2021 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. Climate-related KPIs are reflected in the management team’s performance metrics [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_177]. In 2024, Samsung Electronics reported market-based Scope 1 and 2 emissions of 14.55 million tonnes CO₂e [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_40]. For comparative context, 2023 market-based Scope 1 and 2 emissions were 13,291 thousand tonnes CO₂e (i.e., 13.291 million tonnes CO₂e) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_151]. The baseline year and absolute target for GHG reduction (e.g., science-based target) are not disclosed [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_40]. The renewable energy transition rate was 24.8% in 2024 and targeted at 26% for 2025, but no long-term procurement target (e.g., 100% by a given year) or baseline year is provided [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_40]. The process and frequency of formal Board performance evaluation are not disclosed [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_171]. Director remuneration policies, decision-making processes, and alignment with sustainability goals are not disclosed [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_171]. Verification statements for Scope 3 emissions are included in the report appendix, but the scope, boundaries, and assurance level applied to Scope 3 verification are not described in the source material [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_171].

### Not covered in source material  
The source material does not disclose: (1) formal evaluation of the Board’s own performance, including process or frequency (GRI 2-18); (2) remuneration policies, decision-making process, or annual total compensation ratio for directors (GRI 2-19–2-21); (3) collective knowledge profile of the Board beyond general functional domains (e.g., climate-specific expertise quantification or mapping against TCFD recommendations) (GRI 2-17); (4) scope, boundaries, or assurance level applied to Scope 3 emissions verification (GRI 205-1); (5) confirmed incidents of corruption, outcomes, or corrective measures (GRI 205-3); (6) tax governance structure, control mechanisms, or country-by-country reporting details (GRI 207-2–207-4); (7) science-based or absolute GHG reduction target with baseline year and deadline (TCFD Recommendation g); (8) long-term renewable energy procurement target with baseline year (TCFD Recommendation g); (9) quantified financial targets for climate risk mitigation or opportunity capture (TCFD Recommendation g).

### Energy Performance  
Samsung Electronics reported total energy consumption at business sites of 38,772 GWh in 2024 (DX Division: 4,180 GWh; DS Division: 34,592 GWh) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Electricity accounted for 32,084 GWh (82.7%) of this total, while other energy sources—including steam, LNG, LPG, petrol, and diesel—contributed 6,688 GWh [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Renewable energy consumption was 10,069 GWh in 2024, representing a renewable energy transition rate of 31.4% — defined as *renewable energy consumption (GWh) ÷ total energy consumption at business sites (GWh)* [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. This 31.4% figure is explicitly reported and internally consistent with the disclosed numerator (10,069 GWh) and denominator (32,022 GWh implied by calculation: 10,069 ÷ 0.314 ≈ 32,022), indicating that the denominator used in the official transition rate excludes “Others” (steam, LNG, etc.) — a methodological nuance confirmed by the footnote stating “Renewable energy transition rate % = Renewable energy consumption GWh / Energy consumption at business sites (GWh)” and clarifying that “Energy consumption at business sites” comprises electricity *plus* “Others” [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. However, the arithmetic 10,069 ÷ 38,772 = 25.9% reflects inclusion of all energy forms; the 31.4% rate therefore applies to electricity + “Others” *as defined in the report’s energy accounting framework*, not the full 38,772 GWh aggregate. By division, the DX Division consumed 2,884 GWh of renewable energy out of 3,088 GWh of electricity — a 93.4% renewable electricity rate — while its total energy consumption (electricity + others) was 4,180 GWh, meaning the “others” component (1,092 GWh) is non-electric and not covered by the 93.4% metric [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. The DS Division consumed 7,184 GWh of renewable energy out of 28,996 GWh of electricity (24.8% renewable electricity) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. The company confirmed 100% renewable electricity usage across manufacturing sites in Korea, Vietnam, China, Brazil, Mexico, and India since 2022 via Green Pricing, PPAs (solar/wind), and REC purchases [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_24]. Energy intensity stood at 13.5 MWh per KRW 100 million sales in 2024, calculated as *energy consumption at business sites (MWh) ÷ sales (sales of DX division (absolute value) + sales of DS division (absolute value), KRW 100 million)* [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. Location-based Scope 2 emissions are not disclosed in the source material.

### Water Management  
Total water intake was 188,540,000 tonnes in 2024, comprising 187,639,000 tonnes of municipal (surface) water and 902,000 tonnes of groundwater [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. Wastewater discharge amounted to 152,109,000 tonnes, while water reuse totaled 125,463,000 tonnes—including 74,784,000 tonnes of ultra-pure water supply and 23,025,000 tonnes of recovery [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158]. At Korean manufacturing sites (Giheung, Hwaseong, Pyeongtaek, Cheonan, Onyang), water reuse reached 101,106,000 tonnes in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_65]. This reuse includes internal recirculation of ultra-pure water within semiconductor manufacturing processes and is not drawn from external freshwater sources [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_65]. All Korean sites achieved Alliance for Water Stewardship (AWS) Platinum certification in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Suppliers’ water consumption was reported as 88,467,000 tonnes in 2024, based on the top 90% of suppliers by transaction scale [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158]. Water stress assessments per facility are disclosed qualitatively: Korean sites (Giheung/Hwaseong/Pyeongtaek/Cheonan/Onyang) are classified as “Medium-High”, Xi’an/Suzhou (China) as “Extremely high”, Tianjin (China) as “Medium-High”, and Austin/Taylor (USA) as “Medium-High”, per the Aqueduct Water Risk Atlas standard [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_63]. The report does not disclose numerical WRI Aqueduct scores (e.g., baseline water stress index values) for individual sites.

### Emissions Management  
Market-based Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions totaled 14,546,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024 (Scope 1: 342,000 tonnes; Scope 2: 106,000 tonnes) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. The DS Division’s “region-based” Scope 1 and 2 emissions were reported separately as 15,011,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_152]. This figure exceeds the consolidated market-based total because it represents *DS Division–only* emissions calculated using country-specific electric and fuel emission coefficients (i.e., location-based methodology), whereas the 14,546,000 tonnes CO₂e is the *consolidated group total* under market-based accounting (which incorporates RECs, PPAs, and grid import data) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_152][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. The two figures are not additive nor directly comparable due to differing scopes (DS-only vs. group-wide) and methodologies (location-based vs. market-based); the report does not reconcile them quantitatively. NF₃ emissions—newly disclosed in the 2025 Report—amounted to 1,245,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024 and are included in the total market-based Scope 1 emissions figure [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_152][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. Total Scope 3 emissions were 105,612,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024, with “Use of sold products” constituting 82,714,000 tonnes CO₂e — a decrease of 402,000 tonnes CO₂e from 83,116,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2023, attributed to product energy efficiency improvements [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_154][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_164]. Air pollutant emissions included NOₓ (729 tonnes), SOₓ (35 tonnes), and PM (90 tonnes) in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158]. CH₄ and N₂O emissions are reported in aggregate (CH₄: 1,000 tonnes CO₂e; N₂O: 1,000 tonnes CO₂e) but are not disaggregated by source (e.g., refrigerants, wastewater, leakage) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162].

### Waste Management  
Total waste generated across divisions was 1,348,979 tonnes in 2024 (DX: 322,144 tonnes; DS: 1,026,835 tonnes), comprising general waste (910,510 tonnes), hazardous waste (13,281 tonnes of ferrous metals; 35,909 tonnes of synthetic resin), and other categories [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. In 2024, Samsung collected 690,900 tonnes of e-waste, contributing to a cumulative total of 6,910,000 tonnes recovered from 2009 through end-2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_30]. The company achieved a 99.0% recycling rate at Korean manufacturing sites in 2024, with a target of 99.9% by 2025 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_41]. Twenty-two global sites pursued Platinum Zero Waste-to-Landfill validation, with Korea’s Gumi site and several international locations (e.g., Hungary, Vietnam) already certified Platinum [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_31]. Hazardous waste generation by type (e.g., solvent, heavy metal sludge), landfill diversion rates by site, and e-waste collection volumes by country are not disclosed in the source material.

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
Samsung Electronics integrates climate risk into its enterprise-wide risk management system, applying a four-step process: recognition → assessment → treatment → progress management [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_29][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Physical risks (e.g., drought, flood) and transition risks (e.g., carbon pricing, regulatory shifts) are assessed using IPCC, IEA, and NGFS scenarios [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_46]. Key metrics include Scope 1+2 emissions (target: net zero by 2030 for DX Division; 2050 for DS Division), renewable energy transition rate (target: 100% for all manufacturing sites by 2025), and water reuse (target: 109 million tonnes at Korean sites by 2030) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Financial impact quantification from climate scenarios (e.g., cost implications of drought or carbon pricing) is disclosed qualitatively but not with numerical estimates [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_46][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_20].

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 302 Energy: Location-based Scope 2 emissions breakdown by country; energy from on-site renewables generation (e.g., solar PV capacity); explicit definition of sales metric beyond “sales of DX division (absolute value) + sales of DS division (absolute value), KRW 100 million” — specifically, whether it reflects consolidated revenue under K-IFRS, excludes intercompany sales, or includes non-operating income [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157].

### Occupational Health and Safety  
Samsung Electronics reported a Lost-Time Injury Rate (LTIR) of 0.022% in 2024, down from 0.023% in 2023 and 0.033% in 2022, based on workplace accidents resulting in one or more days of absence (excluding daily life incidents) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146] [GRI 403-9]. The supplier LTIR stood at 0.035% in 2024, a reduction from 0.064% in 2023 and 0.046% in 2022, measured for accidents occurring at Korean suppliers stationed at Samsung’s sites [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146] [GRI 403-7]. No major incidents were recorded in 2022–2024; however, the report does not define “major incident” using an external standard (e.g., ILO Convention No. 187, OSHA fatality/hospitalization thresholds), nor does it disclose whether this reflects zero occurrences or non-reporting due to threshold exclusions [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. The occupational health and safety management system covers all employees globally and extends to suppliers through audits, training, and the Supplier Environmental Safety Portal [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_76][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114] [GRI 403-1, GRI 403-8]. In 2024, approximately 3,000 risk assessment experts were trained to strengthen hazard identification and mitigation capabilities [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_98] [GRI 403-2, GRI 403-5]. Samsung has set a goal to strengthen on-site partner companies’ safety and health capabilities and management systems by 2030 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114] [GRI 403-7]. Specific interventions in business relationships include operating a Work Stoppage Right Research Group with suppliers, supporting consulting and certification assessments for suppliers lacking external OHS certification (e.g., ISO 45001), and delivering special training to strengthen execution capabilities for certified suppliers [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114] [GRI 403-7].

### Training  
In 2024, Samsung Electronics delivered an average of 66.8 training hours per employee globally, up from 58.2 hours in 2023 and 52.1 hours in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147] [GRI 404-1]. In Korea, the average was 61.2 hours per employee, down from 77.5 hours in 2023 and 70.5 hours in 2022 — a 16.3-hour reduction year-on-year — though the context provides no explanation for this decline [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147] [GRI 404-1]. Women received slightly more training than men: 69.0 hours versus 61.6 hours in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147] [GRI 404-1]. Total training expenses amounted to KRW 240.4 billion in 2024 (KRW 100 million × 2,404), representing 0.08% of sales and 0.6% of personnel expenses [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147] [GRI 404-1]. The company operated 936 training sessions globally in 2024, including 522 in Korea and 414 outside Korea [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147] [GRI 404-1]. Human rights training reached 95.7% of all employees in 2024, with offline completion at 98.8% and online at 93.4% [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_77] [GRI 404-1]. No time-bound, quantified target for average training hours (e.g., “achieve 75 hours per employee by 2027”) is disclosed in the source material [GRI 404-2].

### Diversity  
The global percentage of female employees declined to 33.6% in 2024, from 34.0% in 2023 and 35.2% in 2022 — a cumulative decrease of 1.6 percentage points over three years — yet the context offers no analysis of drivers behind this trend [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145] [GRI 405-1]. In Korea, women comprised 25.8% of the workforce in 2024, up from 25.3% in 2023 and 25.2% in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145] [GRI 405-1]. At the executive level, women accounted for 7.4% of executives in 2024, consistent with 7.3% in 2023 and 6.9% in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145] [GRI 405-1]. Employees with disabilities numbered 1,999 in Korea in 2024 (1.9% of the Korean workforce), up from 1,931 (1.8%) in 2023 and 1,732 (1.6%) in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145] [GRI 405-1]. Samsung joined the Valuable 500 initiative in December 2024 to advance inclusion for people with disabilities [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_92] [GRI 405-1]. The ratio of basic salary and remuneration of women to men (GRI 405-2) is not disclosed globally; only regional gender pay gap figures are referenced for the UK, France, and Brazil, with no consolidated global ratio provided [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_95] [GRI 405-2].

### Supplier Social Assessment  
In 2024, 92% of Samsung’s global suppliers underwent comprehensive evaluation, with 75% rated “outstanding” — up from 71% in 2023 and 62% in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_148] [GRI 414-1]. The context does not define the criteria or methodology used to determine “comprehensive evaluation”, nor does it clarify whether the 92% refers to supplier count, spend-weighted coverage, or risk-based sampling [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_148][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_110] [GRI 414-1]. Among first-tier suppliers, 93% complied with working hour standards in 2024, recovering from 85% in 2023 and aligning with 2022’s 93%; the context attributes the 2023 dip to “temporary increase in factory operating rates after the end of the COVID-19 pandemic”, and notes that operations stabilized by 2024, restoring compliance [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114] [GRI 414-2]. Third-party audit compliance rates for non-discrimination stood at 100% for first-tier suppliers in 2024, down from 100% in 2023 but significantly higher than 92% for second-tier suppliers [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_150] [GRI 414-2]. Forced labor special audits covered 53 suppliers across five countries in 2024, and USD 14,838 in recruitment fees was returned to 41 migrant workers [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114] [GRI 414-2]. Corrective actions taken in response to supplier social non-compliance include requiring immediate remediation of serious violations (e.g., child labor, forced labor), verifying completion of corrective action plans within three months of audit finding registration, and conducting follow-up assessments to confirm implementation [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_110] [GRI 414-2].

### TCFD Strategy (Social Impacts of Climate Transition)  
The context confirms Samsung Electronics conducted climate scenario analysis using IPCC, IEA, and NGFS frameworks to assess physical and transition risks and opportunities, including financial impacts on operations, supply chain, and product demand [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_179][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_20] [TCFD Strategy]. It identifies transition opportunities such as “increases in demand for low-carbon products and services” and “use of renewable energy” [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_179] [TCFD Strategy]. However, no disclosure addresses the *social* dimensions of climate transition — including workforce reskilling for green jobs, community engagement in decarbonisation, just transition planning for affected workers or regions, or social safeguards in low-carbon investment decisions — is present in the provided material [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_179] [TCFD Strategy].

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 405-2 (ratio of basic salary and remuneration of women to men) is not disclosed globally; only regional gender pay gap data for the UK, France, and Brazil is referenced without a consolidated global figure [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_95]. GRI 403-7 requires disclosure of prevention and mitigation of occupational health and safety impacts directly linked by business relationships; while supplier LTIR and training initiatives are reported, no data on joint safety protocols co-developed with top-tier suppliers, contractual OHS clauses, or timelines for supplier incident remediation beyond the general “within 3 months” is provided [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_76][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114]. GRI 414-2 (negative social impacts in the supply chain and actions taken) lacks root-cause analyses, outcome metrics (e.g., % of corrective actions verified as effective), or descriptions of capacity-building mandates or contract revisions beyond fee reimbursements and working hour compliance recovery [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_150]. TCFD Strategy disclosures on social impacts of climate transition — including workforce reskilling pathways, community engagement, or just transition planning — are absent from the provided context [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_179]. No time-bound, quantified targets (e.g., “reduce LTIR to 0.015% by 2027”, “achieve 40% female executives by 2030”, “remediate 100% of high-risk supplier findings within 90 days by 2026”) are disclosed for any Social performance indicator.

### Board Composition and Oversight Structure (GRI 2-9, 2-11, 2-12, 2-15, TCFD Governance)  
As of the end of March 2025, Samsung Electronics’ Board of Directors comprises 3 internal directors and 6 independent directors, with the roles of Board Chair and CEO formally separated to strengthen independence and transparency; independent director Je-Yoon Shin serves as Chair [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5] (GRI 2-11). The Board’s collective expertise includes individuals with extensive knowledge or experience in finance, law, IT (robotics, AI, semiconductors), risk management, public sector, and sustainable management — reflecting deliberate consideration of functional diversity, gender, and nationality in director appointments [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5] (GRI 2-9). Two of the six independent directors are women, supporting balanced decision-making [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5] (GRI 2-9). All independent directors serve on the Sustainability Committee — a dedicated committee under the Board established in July 2021 to oversee environmental, social, and governance (ESG) strategy, risk management, and shareholder value creation [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5] (GRI 2-16). The Board approves long-term environmental strategies such as the “New Environmental Strategy”, resolved in September 2022, which encompasses climate change response and resource circularity goals [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_177][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_11] (TCFD Governance a, GRI 2-12). Since 2023, key achievements related to these goals have been reviewed annually by the Sustainability Committee as part of its formal agenda [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_11][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_40] (GRI 2-16). Conflicts of interest are addressed through documented policies and oversight mechanisms [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_171] (GRI 2-15).

### Anti-Corruption Governance and Compliance Systems (GRI 205-1, 205-2, 205-3)  
Samsung Electronics maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward corruption and bribery, grounded in its Global Anti-Corruption and Bribery Policy [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133] (GRI 205-1). The corporate Compliance Team, led by the Chief Compliance Officer, attends all Board and Management Committee meetings to support transparent decision-making and reports major issues directly to the Board [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133] (GRI 205-1). The Samsung Compliance Committee — an independent external body launched in February 2020 — advises seven major Samsung Group member companies, including Samsung Electronics, on strengthening compliance monitoring and control functions [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133] (GRI 205-1). In 2024, anti-corruption was explicitly cited as a focus area in compliance audits of global manufacturing sites (Q3) and external technology sourcing channels (Q4) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137] (GRI 205-1). A total of 1,238 compliance-related whistleblowing cases and 930 ethics-related cases were reported in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137] (GRI 205-2). All employees — including contract and part-time workers — receive annual compliance training covering anti-corruption and fair trade; in 2024, 138,414 individuals completed such training [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137] (GRI 205-2). Confirmed incidents of corruption and actions taken are not disclosed in the source material [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_173] (GRI 205-3). The operational reason for non-disclosure is not stated in the provided context; no timeline for future disclosure is indicated.

### Integration of Climate Risk into Enterprise Risk Management (TCFD Governance & Risk Management, GRI 2-12, 2-13)  
Climate-related risks and opportunities are systematically integrated into Samsung Electronics’ enterprise risk management system [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181] (TCFD Risk Management c, GRI 2-13). The company employs a structured Climate-Related Risk and Opportunity Analysis Process that includes forming a risk/opportunity pool, conducting scenario analysis (using IPCC, IEA, and NGFS scenarios), assessing financial impacts, and evaluating mitigation and adaptation capacity [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_44][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18] (TCFD Risk Management b). Physical risks (e.g., floods, typhoons, droughts, wildfires, extreme heat) impact operations across short-, medium-, and long-term horizons, while transition risks (e.g., rising carbon credit costs, energy price volatility) and opportunities (e.g., demand for low-carbon products, renewable energy adoption) predominantly affect the medium- to long-term [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_178][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_43] (TCFD Risk Management a). Key findings from this analysis are reported to the Sustainability Committee and ESG Management Council for deliberation and response planning [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181] (TCFD Governance a, GRI 2-12).
